# Multi-omics ordination {#sec-unsupervised-multiomics}


In this chapter, we continue from where we left off in the previous section
([@sec-cross-correlation]). Instead of testing feature pairs one by one, we
now look for patterns that are shared across the omic layers. We introduce two
unsupervised integration methods: Joint Robust Principal Component Analysis
(Joint-RPCA) [@CordazzoVargas2026] and Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA)
[@Argelaguet2018].

Both methods are based on ordination, similar to principal component
analysis (PCA) and principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) introduced in
[@sec-community-similarity]. They reduce the dimensionality of the data into a
small number of components or factors that capture the main patterns of
variation. Unlike in single-table ordination, these components are shared
across the omic layers, and each feature in each layer gets a loading or
weight on them. Features with large loadings on the same component co-vary
across the samples.

However, the methods make different assumptions about the data:

- **Joint-RPCA** extends robust PCA (RPCA) [@Martino2019] to multiple tables.
  It assumes that the tables share an underlying low-rank structure that can
  be estimated with matrix completion. Microbiome data is transformed with the
  robust centered log-ratio (rclr) transformation, in which zeros are treated
  as missing values. This makes
  the method designed for sparse and compositional data. In the benchmarks of
  @CordazzoVargas2026, Joint-RPCA recovered phenotype-associated structure
  more consistently than general-purpose multi-omics methods, including MOFA,
  under the sparse and compositional data conditions typical of microbiome
  studies.

- **MOFA** is a probabilistic factor model that does not assume any
  microbiome-specific data properties. By default, it assumes normally
  distributed data, so the data is usually transformed and standardized
  beforehand. MOFA is a general-purpose method that is widely used in
  multi-omics studies across fields, and it is supported by a large set of
  tools and tutorials. When the data matches its assumptions, it can perform
  better than Joint-RPCA [@CordazzoVargas2026].

## Data

We use the @Hintikka2021 dataset introduced in [@sec-global-association].

```{r}
#| label: unsupervised_data

library(mia)

data("HintikkaXOData", package = "mia")
mae <- HintikkaXOData
```

For Joint-RPCA, we agglomerate the microbiome data to genus level and filter
the counts in three steps, in the same order as
[gemelli](https://github.com/biocore/gemelli), the original Python
implementation of Joint-RPCA: we remove genera with few reads, then genera that
are present in few samples, and finally samples with few reads.
Each step is computed from the data left by the previous step, so, for
instance, library sizes are calculated after the rare genera are removed.
Filtering must be done on untransformed counts. Then, we apply the rclr
transformation. We set `impute = FALSE`, because Joint-RPCA handles the zeros,
i.e., missing values, itself through matrix completion. The metabolite
concentrations are log10-transformed. The biomarker data contains zeros, so
instead of a log transformation, we standardize each biomarker.

```{r}
#| label: jrpca_preprocess

# Agglomerate microbiome data
mae[["microbiota"]] <- agglomerateByRank(mae[["microbiota"]], rank = "Genus")
# Remove the "D_5__" prefix of the SILVA genus names to shorten the labels
rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]) <- sub(
    "^D_5__", "", rownames(mae[["microbiota"]])
)

# Filter the raw counts in steps
tse <- mae[["microbiota"]]
# 1. Remove genera with 10 reads or fewer in total
tse <- tse[rowSums(assay(tse, "counts")) > 10, ]
# 2. Remove genera that are present in 10% or less of the samples
tse <- tse[rowMeans(assay(tse, "counts") > 0) > 0.1, ]
# 3. Remove samples with 1000 reads or fewer
tse <- tse[, colSums(assay(tse, "counts")) > 1000]
mae[["microbiota"]] <- tse

# Apply rclr transformation without imputing zeros
mae[["microbiota"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["microbiota"]],
    method = "rclr",
    impute = FALSE
)

# Apply log10 transformation to metabolome NMR assay
mae[["metabolites"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["metabolites"]],
    assay.type = "nmr",
    method = "log10"
)

# Standardize biomarker assay
mae[["biomarkers"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["biomarkers"]],
    assay.type = "signals",
    method = "standardize",
    MARGIN = "rows"
)
```

::: callout-note
## Note: Filtering with mia functions

The metrics can also be calculated with `getPrevalence()` and `addQC()` from
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")`. If so, recalculate them after each step: metrics
calculated once from the original object ignore the earlier steps, e.g.,
library sizes would still include the reads of the removed genera.
:::

## Joint-RPCA {#sec-joint-rpca}

Joint-RPCA (joint robust principal component analysis) is available in
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")` and its results can be visualized with
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("miaViz")`. We run the analysis with
`addJointRPCA()`, which stores the results in the `metadata` of the
`MultiAssayExperiment` [@Ramos2017].

```{r}
#| label: jrpca_run

set.seed(123)
mae <- addJointRPCA(
    mae,
    experiments = c("microbiota", "metabolites", "biomarkers"),
    assay.types = c("rclr", "log10", "standardize"),
    ncomponents = 5
)

# Sample scores
metadata(mae)[["JointRPCA"]] |> head()
```

The explained variance is visualized with `plotJointRPCAExplainedVariance()`.
The heatmap shows how the variance of each omic layer is divided across the
components, and the barplot shows how the total variance is divided across
the layers. Note that the values describe the low-rank Joint-RPCA model,
not the proportion of variance explained in the observed data
(@fig-jrpca-variance).

```{r}
#| label: fig-jrpca-variance
#| fig-cap: "Variance explained by the Joint-RPCA model of the Hintikka et al. (2021) data. The heatmap shows the variance of each omic layer (microbiota, metabolites, biomarkers) explained by each of the five components, and the barplot shows the share of total variance per layer."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels: a heatmap with the five Joint-RPCA components against the microbiota, metabolite and biomarker layers, filled by the variance explained, and a barplot with one bar per omic layer showing its share of the total variance."
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10

library(miaViz)

plotJointRPCAExplainedVariance(mae, "JointRPCA", add.total = TRUE)
```

As in other ordination methods, the samples can be visualized in the space of
the first two components (@fig-jrpca-ordination).

```{r}
#| label: fig-jrpca-ordination
#| fig-cap: "Joint-RPCA sample scores of the Hintikka et al. (2021) data on the first two components, colored by diet."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of samples on Joint-RPCA component 1 (x-axis) and component 2 (y-axis), with points colored by diet."

plotJointRPCA(mae, "JointRPCA", colour.by = "Diet")
```

We can then visualize the features with the largest loadings in each omic
layer for the first two components to analyze co-varying features
(@fig-jrpca-loadings).

```{r}
#| label: fig-jrpca-loadings
#| fig-cap: "Top 10 features with the largest Joint-RPCA loadings on the first two components in each omic layer (microbiota genera, metabolites and biomarkers) of the Hintikka et al. (2021) data."
#| fig-alt: "Grid of horizontal bar charts, one per omic layer and component, each listing the ten microbiota genera, metabolites or biomarkers with the largest loadings on components 1 and 2 and the size and sign of each loading."
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 10
#| column: page

plotJointRPCALoadings(mae, "JointRPCA", ncomponents = 2, n = 10)
```

In addition to the loadings, the co-variation can be visualized directly as
correlations between features both within and across the omic layers. The
correlations are calculated from the Joint-RPCA model, and they reflect how
the features align in the Joint-RPCA space rather than correlations in the
observed data (@fig-jrpca-covariance).

```{r}
#| label: fig-jrpca-covariance
#| fig-cap: "Heatmap of correlations between the top features of the microbiota, metabolite and biomarker layers, derived from the Joint-RPCA model of the Hintikka et al. (2021) data."
#| fig-alt: "Square heatmap with the top features of the microbiota, metabolite and biomarker layers on both axes, where cell color shows the correlation between each pair of features within and across layers."
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 9
#| column: page

plotJointRPCACovariance(mae, "JointRPCA", ntop = 10, correlation = TRUE)
```

The same information can be visualized as a network, where the edges connect
strongly correlated features (@fig-jrpca-network).

```{r}
#| label: fig-jrpca-network
#| fig-cap: "Network of features from the microbiota, metabolite and biomarker layers based on the Joint-RPCA model of the Hintikka et al. (2021) data. Edges connect strongly correlated features."
#| fig-alt: "Network graph whose labelled nodes are features from the microbiota, metabolite and biomarker layers, joined by edges between strongly correlated features."
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 9

plotJointRPCANetwork(mae, "JointRPCA", show.label = TRUE)
```

## MOFA {#sec-mofa}

Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA) is an unsupervised method for integrating
multi-omic datasets in a downstream analysis [@Argelaguet2018]. It could be
seen as a generalization of principal component analysis, with the ability
to infer a latent (low-dimensional) representation shared among the multiple
(-omics) datasets in hand.

We use the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("MOFA2")` package [@Argelaguet2020] for
analysis.

```{r}
#| label: mofa_data1

library(mia)

# Import dataset
data("HintikkaXOData", package = "mia")

# Store as mae
mae <- HintikkaXOData
```

The `mae` object could be used directly to create the MOFA model. Yet,
we transform our assays since the model assumes normality by
default, and the Gaussian model is recommended
(see [MOFA2 FAQ](https://biofam.github.io/MOFA2/faq.html)). However, Poisson and
Bernoulli distribution models are also available.

```{r}
#| label: mofa2
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(MOFA2)

# Agglomerate microbiome data
mae[[1]] <- agglomerateByRank(mae[[1]], rank = "Genus")
rownames(mae[[1]]) <- sub("^D_5__", "", rownames(mae[[1]]))
mae[[1]] <- addPrevalence(mae[[1]])
mae[[1]] <- subsetBy(
    mae[[1]],
    rows = prevalence > 0.5, collapse = TRUE
)

# Apply CLR transformation to microbiome counts assay
mae[[1]] <- transformAssay(mae[[1]], method = "clr", pseudocount = TRUE)

# Standardize microbiome CLR assay
mae[[1]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[[1]],
    assay.type = "clr",
    method = "standardize",
    MARGIN = "rows",
    name = "clr-z"
)

# Apply log10 transformation to metabolome NMR assay
mae[[2]] <- transformAssay(mae[[2]], assay.type = "nmr", method = "log10")

# Standardize metabolome log10 assay
mae[[2]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[[2]],
    assay.type = "log10",
    method = "standardize",
    MARGIN = "rows",
    name = "log10-z"
)

# Standardize biomarker assay
mae[[3]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[[3]],
    assay.type = "signals",
    method = "standardize",
    MARGIN = "rows",
    name = "z"
)
```

Then, we prepare the MOFA2 model and define the data and training parameters
available as additional arguments, which will otherwise be set to default
values.
The full parameter list can be found with `?mofa2`.

```{r}
#| label: mofa4

# Build MOFA2 model
model <- mofa2(
    mae,
    experiments = c("microbiota", "metabolites", "biomarkers"),
    assays = c("clr-z", "log10-z", "z"),
    num_factors = 5
)

# View model
model
```

The model is then trained with `run_mofa`.

```{r}
#| label: mofa5
#| results: false

# Some systems may require the specification `use_basilisk = TRUE`
# so it has been added to the following code
model <- run_mofa(model, use_basilisk = TRUE)
```

The explained variance is visualized with the `plot_variance_explained()`
function (@fig-mofa-variance).

```{r}
#| label: fig-mofa-variance
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"
#| fig-cap: "Variance explained by the MOFA model of the Hintikka et al. (2021) data. The heatmap shows the variance explained per factor (rows) and omic layer (columns), and the barplot shows the total variance explained per layer."
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked panels: a heatmap of MOFA factors (rows) against the omic layers (columns), filled by the variance explained, and a barplot of the total variance explained in each layer."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 10
#| column: page

library(patchwork)

plot_list <- plot_variance_explained(
    model,
    x = "view", y = "factor",
    plot_total = TRUE
)

wrap_plots(plot_list, nrow = 2)
```

Similarly to Joint-RPCA, the samples can be visualized in the space of the
first two factors (@fig-mofa-factors).

```{r}
#| label: fig-mofa-factors
#| fig-cap: "MOFA sample scores of the Hintikka et al. (2021) data on factors 1 and 2, colored by diet."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of samples on MOFA factor 1 (x-axis) and factor 2 (y-axis), with points colored by diet."

plot_factors(model, factors = c(1, 2), color_by = "Diet")
```

We can then visualize the top weights for microbiota and metabolites for
the first two factors to analyze co-varying features (@fig-mofa-weights).

```{r}
#| label: fig-mofa-weights
#| fig-cap: "Top 10 features with the largest absolute MOFA weights on factors 1 and 2 for the microbiota (top) and metabolite (bottom) layers of the Hintikka et al. (2021) data."
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked rows of panels for factors 1 and 2, showing the ten microbiota features (top) and the ten metabolites (bottom) with the largest absolute weights, each drawn as a point along the weight axis."
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 10
#| column: page

p1 <- plot_top_weights(
    model,
    view = "microbiota",
    factors = c(1, 2),
    nfeatures = 10
)

p2 <- plot_top_weights(
    model,
    view = "metabolites",
    factors = c(1, 2),
    nfeatures = 10
)

wrap_plots(p1 + ggtitle("Microbiota"), p2 + ggtitle("Metabolites"), ncol = 1)
```

More tutorials and examples of using the package are found at
[MOFA2 tutorials](https://biofam.github.io/MOFA2/tutorials.html).

## Exercises {#sec-unsupervised-multiomics-exercises}

We use the [`HintikkaXOData`](data_sets.qmd#sec-data-hintikka) dataset, as in
this chapter.

Solve the exercises in order, as each exercise continues from the previous
one. Try to solve each exercise yourself before opening the solution.

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 1: Shared components

**Goal:** Explain what the ordination-based integration methods estimate and how
Joint-RPCA and MOFA differ.

Answer the following questions without writing any code. The beginning of
this chapter will help you.

1. How do Joint-RPCA and MOFA differ from a PCA that is run on a single
table?

2. A bacterial genus and a metabolite both have a large positive loading on
the first component. What does this tell about them?

3. How does the rclr transformation used in Joint-RPCA handle zeros? Why does
this suit microbiome data?

4. Why is the data usually transformed and standardized before running MOFA?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

1. Like PCA, they reduce the data into a small number of components or
factors that capture the main patterns of variation. Unlike in single-table
PCA, the components are shared across the omic layers, and each feature in
each layer gets a loading or weight on them.

2. Features with large loadings on the same component co-vary across the
samples. Here, samples with a high score on the first component tend to have
high values of both the genus and the metabolite.

3. The rclr transformation treats zeros as missing values, and Joint-RPCA
estimates them with matrix completion. Microbiome data is sparse and
compositional, so it has many zeros that may not be true absences. The method
is designed for these properties.

4. By default, MOFA assumes normally distributed data, and it does not assume
any microbiome-specific properties. The transformations make the data closer
to normal, and the standardization puts all features on the same scale.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 2: Prepare the data for Joint-RPCA

**Goal:** Prepare multi-omic data for Joint-RPCA.

1. Load the `HintikkaXOData` dataset from the `mia` package and store it in a
variable called `mae`.

2. Check which experiments the dataset contains and which assays each
experiment has.

3. Agglomerate the microbiota data to genus level.

4. Filter the `counts` assay of the microbiota data in three steps: remove the
genera with 10 reads or fewer in total, then the genera that are present in
10% or less of the samples, and finally the samples with 1000 reads or fewer.
How many genera and samples remain?

5. Apply the rclr transformation to the microbiota data without imputing the
zeros (`impute = FALSE`).

6. Count the zeros in the `counts` assay and the missing values in the `rclr`
assay of the microbiota data. Compare the two numbers.

7. Apply the log10 transformation to the `nmr` assay of the metabolites, and
standardize each biomarker in the `signals` assay.

**Useful functions:** `data()`, `MultiAssayExperiment::experiments()`,
`assayNames()`, `mia::agglomerateByRank()`, `assay()`, `rowSums()`,
`rowMeans()`, `colSums()`, `dim()`, `mia::transformAssay()`, `is.na()`,
`sum()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_multiomics_prepare

library(mia)

# 1. Load the data
data("HintikkaXOData", package = "mia")
mae <- HintikkaXOData

# 2. Experiments and their assays
experiments(mae)
assayNames(mae[["microbiota"]])
assayNames(mae[["metabolites"]])
assayNames(mae[["biomarkers"]])

# 3. Agglomerate the microbiota data to genus level
mae[["microbiota"]] <- agglomerateByRank(mae[["microbiota"]], rank = "Genus")
rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]) <-
    sub("^D_5__", "", rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]))

# 4. Filter the counts in three steps
tse <- mae[["microbiota"]]
tse <- tse[rowSums(assay(tse, "counts")) > 10, ]
tse <- tse[rowMeans(assay(tse, "counts") > 0) > 0.1, ]
tse <- tse[, colSums(assay(tse, "counts")) > 1000]
mae[["microbiota"]] <- tse
dim(mae[["microbiota"]])

# 5. rclr transformation without imputing zeros
mae[["microbiota"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["microbiota"]],
    method = "rclr",
    impute = FALSE
)

# 6. Zeros in counts and missing values in rclr
sum(assay(mae[["microbiota"]], "counts") == 0)
sum(is.na(assay(mae[["microbiota"]], "rclr")))

# 7. Transform metabolites and biomarkers
mae[["metabolites"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["metabolites"]],
    assay.type = "nmr",
    method = "log10"
)
mae[["biomarkers"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["biomarkers"]],
    assay.type = "signals",
    method = "standardize",
    MARGIN = "rows"
)
```

6. The two numbers are equal, because each zero in the counts becomes a
missing value in the rclr assay. Joint-RPCA estimates these missing values
itself.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 3: Run Joint-RPCA

**Goal:** Run Joint-RPCA and visualize the explained variance and the samples.

1. Set the seed to 123 and run Joint-RPCA with `addJointRPCA()` on all three
experiments. Use the assays `rclr`, `log10` and `standardize`, and three
components (`ncomponents = 3`).

2. Show the first sample scores, which are stored in `metadata(mae)`.

3. Visualize the explained variance.

4. Plot the samples in the space of the first two components, and color them
by `Diet`.

5. How do you read the explained variance plot? How can you see from the
sample plot whether the diet groups differ?

**Useful functions:** `set.seed()`, `mia::addJointRPCA()`, `metadata()`,
`head()`, `miaViz::plotJointRPCAExplainedVariance()`,
`miaViz::plotJointRPCA()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_multiomics_jrpca

library(miaViz)

# 1. Run Joint-RPCA with three components
set.seed(123)
mae <- addJointRPCA(
    mae,
    experiments = c("microbiota", "metabolites", "biomarkers"),
    assay.types = c("rclr", "log10", "standardize"),
    ncomponents = 3
)

# 2. Sample scores
metadata(mae)[["JointRPCA"]] |> head()

# 3. Explained variance
plotJointRPCAExplainedVariance(mae, "JointRPCA", add.total = TRUE)

# 4. Samples colored by diet
plotJointRPCA(mae, "JointRPCA", colour.by = "Diet")
```

5. The heatmap shows how the variance of each omic layer is divided across
the components, and the barplot shows how the total variance is divided
across the layers. A component that explains much variance in several layers
captures a pattern that is shared by them. Note that the values describe the
low-rank Joint-RPCA model, not the observed data. In the sample plot, each
point is a sample. If the colors form separate groups along a component, that
component captures differences between the diet groups.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 4: Co-varying features in Joint-RPCA

**Goal:** Find features that co-vary across the omic layers.

1. Visualize the ten features with the largest loadings on the first two
components in each omic layer.

2. Visualize the correlations between the top ten features of each layer as a
heatmap (`ntop = 10`, `correlation = TRUE`).

3. Visualize the same correlations as a network with feature labels.

4. How do you read the heatmap and the network? Are these correlations
calculated from the observed data?

**Useful functions:** `miaViz::plotJointRPCALoadings()`,
`miaViz::plotJointRPCACovariance()`, `miaViz::plotJointRPCANetwork()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_multiomics_jrpca_features
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

# 1. Top loadings in each omic layer
plotJointRPCALoadings(mae, "JointRPCA", ncomponents = 2, n = 10)

# 2. Correlations between the top features as a heatmap
plotJointRPCACovariance(mae, "JointRPCA", ntop = 10, correlation = TRUE)

# 3. Correlations as a network
plotJointRPCANetwork(mae, "JointRPCA", show.label = TRUE)
```

4. In the heatmap, each cell shows the correlation between two features,
both within and across the omic layers. Positive values mean that the features
increase together, and negative values that one increases when the other
decreases. In the network, the nodes are features and the edges connect
strongly correlated features. The correlations are not calculated from the
observed data. They are derived from the Joint-RPCA model and describe how the
features align in the Joint-RPCA space.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 5: Run MOFA

**Goal:** Prepare the data for MOFA, train the model and visualize the results.

1. Load `HintikkaXOData` again and store it in `mae`, so that you start from
the original data.

2. Agglomerate the microbiota data to the Genus rank. Then add the
prevalence, and combine the genera with a prevalence of 0.5 or less into
"Other". Apply the CLR transformation with
`pseudocount = TRUE`, and then standardize each genus. Store the
standardized assay under the name `"clr-z"`.

3. Apply the log10 transformation to the `nmr` assay of the metabolites, and
then standardize each metabolite. Store the standardized assay under the name
`"log10-z"`.

4. Standardize each biomarker in the `signals` assay, and store the result
under the name `"z"`.

5. Create a MOFA model with `mofa2()` from the three experiments and the
assays `clr-z`, `log10-z` and `z`, with three factors (`num_factors = 3`).
Train the model with `run_mofa()` and `use_basilisk = TRUE`.

6. Visualize the explained variance per factor and omic layer, with the
layers on the x-axis and the factors on the y-axis. Then, in a separate plot,
visualize the total variance explained in each layer.

7. Plot the samples in the space of the first two factors, and color them by
`Diet`.

8. Visualize the ten features with the largest weights on the first two
factors for the microbiota. Then make the same plot for the metabolites.

9. Compare the sample plot and the top features to those from Joint-RPCA in
Exercises 3 and 4. Why might the two methods give different results?

**Useful functions:** `mia::agglomerateByRank()`, `mia::addPrevalence()`,
`mia::subsetBy()`,
`mia::transformAssay()`, `MOFA2::mofa2()`, `MOFA2::run_mofa()`,
`MOFA2::plot_variance_explained()`, `MOFA2::plot_factors()`,
`MOFA2::plot_top_weights()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_multiomics_mofa
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: hide

library(MOFA2)

# 1. Load the original data
data("HintikkaXOData", package = "mia")
mae <- HintikkaXOData

# 2. Microbiota: prevalent genera, CLR and standardization
mae[["microbiota"]] <- agglomerateByRank(
    mae[["microbiota"]],
    rank = "Genus"
)
rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]) <-
    sub("^D_5__", "", rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]))
mae[["microbiota"]] <- addPrevalence(mae[["microbiota"]])
mae[["microbiota"]] <- subsetBy(
    mae[["microbiota"]],
    rows = prevalence > 0.5,
    collapse = TRUE
)
mae[["microbiota"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["microbiota"]],
    method = "clr",
    pseudocount = TRUE
)
mae[["microbiota"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["microbiota"]],
    assay.type = "clr",
    method = "standardize",
    MARGIN = "rows",
    name = "clr-z"
)

# 3. Metabolites: log10 and standardization
mae[["metabolites"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["metabolites"]],
    assay.type = "nmr",
    method = "log10"
)
mae[["metabolites"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["metabolites"]],
    assay.type = "log10",
    method = "standardize",
    MARGIN = "rows",
    name = "log10-z"
)

# 4. Biomarkers: standardization
mae[["biomarkers"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["biomarkers"]],
    assay.type = "signals",
    method = "standardize",
    MARGIN = "rows",
    name = "z"
)

# 5. Create and train the MOFA model
model <- mofa2(
    mae,
    experiments = c("microbiota", "metabolites", "biomarkers"),
    assays = c("clr-z", "log10-z", "z"),
    num_factors = 3
)
model <- run_mofa(model, use_basilisk = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: exercise_multiomics_mofa_plots
#| warning: false

# 6. Explained variance per factor and layer, and in total
plot_list <- plot_variance_explained(
    model,
    x = "view", y = "factor",
    plot_total = TRUE
)
plot_list[[1]]
plot_list[[2]]

# 7. Samples colored by diet
plot_factors(model, factors = c(1, 2), color_by = "Diet")

# 8. Top weights for the microbiota and the metabolites
plot_top_weights(model, view = "microbiota", factors = c(1, 2), nfeatures = 10)
plot_top_weights(model, view = "metabolites", factors = c(1, 2), nfeatures = 10)
```

9. Compare whether the diet groups are separated along the first components
or factors in both methods, and which features have the largest loadings or
weights in both. Note that the sign and order of the components can differ
between the methods. The methods can give different results, because they
use different transformations and assumptions. Joint-RPCA uses the rclr
transformation, treats zeros as missing values and is designed for sparse and
compositional data. MOFA assumes normally distributed data, and the
microbiota data was CLR-transformed with a pseudocount and standardized. Also
the filtering of the genera differed between the methods.
